{"id": "2:61/q18", "question": "What does baql mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q18/p1", "position": "Fresh plants and edible greens", "reasons": "IBNABIHATIM (قتادة): When they reached Syria and missed their former foods, they asked Moses to seek vegetables from the earth for them. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (أبو النجم): Abu al-Najm’s poem uses tabaqqalat for camels grazing at the first sprouting of vegetation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن دريد): Baql is a genus covering fresh growth eaten by people and animals; the land verbs mean that the land has become vegetated, and Ibn Durayd connects al-bāqillāʾ to it. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The phrase من بقلها is an appositive to مما تنبت الأرض with the preposition repeated, a fluent construction. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa allows من بقلها to explain the kind and treats it as an accusative circumstantial phrase from an omitted pronoun. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (المهدوي وابن عطية): Al-Mahdawi and Ibn Atiyya call من بقلها an appositive even though they take the two prepositions to have different senses. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزمخشري): The greens mean choice vegetables people eat, such as mint, celery, and leek. SAMIN-DURR: من بقلها may be an appositive to ما with the preposition repeated, where من explains the kind. SAMIN-DURR: بقل is all plant growth without a stem, and its plural is بقول. IBNKATHIR-FULL (عبد الله بن مسعود): Ibn Masud reports that Israelites killed three hundred prophets in one day, then sold vegetables in the market at day's end. BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says baql is the growth of the earth that supplements fatty foods; the author first identifies it as greens. DURR-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud says Israelites killed three hundred prophets in a day and sold vegetables in the market by evening.
